Cat 8 can handle frequencies up to 2000 MHz and is capable of delivering 25Gbps or 40Gbps over distances of up to 30 meters. However, to reach the 100Gbps mark, you would typically need to employ a technology called Multi-Gigabit Ethernet, which utilizes a combination of advanced signaling techniques and higher-grade cabling. Another option is to use a technology called 100GBASE-T, which allows for 100Gbps transmission over twisted pair cabling, but it generally requires a more robust infrastructure and may have distance limitations compared to fiber optics. While copper solutions can be more cost-effective and easier to install in certain environments, they do come with challenges such as increased electromagnetic interference and attenuation over longer distances. Therefore, while it’s feasible to implement a 100Gb network with copper wire, careful planning and consideration of the specific requirements of your network environment are essential to ensure optimal performance. Question: Do DVB-T2 standard support satelite DVB-S2 and vice versa? If not, why do all TV makers ditching DVB-S2 first?
Old_Answer: Satellite signals generally use PSK modulation and terrestrial signals use a more complex form of QAM. Satellite signals are very much more subject to noise because they get huge amounts of attenuation over the massive distances they're sent (and wide distribution). Terrestrial signals are less prone to this and have stronger signals, but they're subject to a great deal of reflection and instantaneous noise. They implement not dissimilar techniques but they come at it from a very different objective to deal with very different environments. Importantly, the chips are optimised to fixed function. Making the processing be more flexible means making them more complex. Additionally, if you add components for dealing with driving the satellite LNB, you're spending money and if it's not going to be used, that's money for nothing. In most countries, satellite TV is exclusively pay TV and heavily dependent on a separate set-top box. So the use of satellite for TVs directly is limited. But terrestrial is far more common for free to view TV.
Answer_with_writing_sample: The DVB-T2 and DVB-S2 standards serve different purposes and are not directly compatible with each other.
